utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Which year are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: In 1991, for the most part, duty had been stepped up at the operations centre, in view of the many tasks that were later foisted on us, so there were two further administrators working there for the rear, from the operations organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell me what one can find in the rooms of the operational centre of the 9th VPS command at Kumbor?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: In the rooms of the 9th VPS command centre, there is a switchboard, the duty-officer, like a small switchboard, it's a desk, and there's an STINA computer system, which has a direct link with the monitoring radar, the Falcon monitoring radar, and this is used for automatic monitoring of the situation on the surface. Then there is a planchet for manual monitoring of the situation on the surface and another planchet for the monitoring of air targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we just have this confirmed, please. At the operations centre you have a duty desk with telephone communication lines, if I understand you correctly.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Telephone communication lines only for a situation where this is the only switchboard. In view of the fact that military communications with Croatia had been cut, and this was the only switchboard through which one could establish communication with the units that were in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. What about the operational centre? Was there a department there where you had radio communications?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Yes. We had radio communications, and the radio network was always open. This was used for the salvaging of vessels at sea and for emergency situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me: In what way could one establish a link with the units in Croatia and the forward command post at Kupari, or with Trebinje, for example?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Only through us. Therefore, they called us and we were the switchboard that put them through to whoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say "through us," can you specify, please.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Through the desk, or switchboard. It was some sort of a switchboard, and as soon as someone called and asked to be put through to a certain unit or the forward command post, or someone else who was at the BIS, we were able to put them through.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Therefore, it was only through the operational centre at Kumbor that this would have been possible?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about the other way around? What I want to know is whether the Kupari forward command post could have a direct link with the units in Croatia, or specifically, with Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about the operations group at Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: No. Only through us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir: How would they establish communication from the ford command post at Kupari with the command of the operations group in Trebinje? In what way? Can you explain, please.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: They would call us. It's as simple as that. I tell him to hold, then I would call the operations centre in Trebinje and I would put him through.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would it be done the same way if Trebinje asked to speak to the forward command post at Kupari?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Yes, in the very same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about the Kupari forward command post? Can they establish a direct link with Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: No. Only through us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I assume the same applies to the situation the other way around, doesn't it. Belgrade and the forward command post at Kupari?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: First and foremost, I want to know about the period between October and December 1991. Tell us, sir: Did you spend this whole period of time at Kumbor?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Yes, the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir: What sort of activities were carried out at the VPS command at Kumbor as at the time you had a forward command post at Kupari?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: In addition to the basic tasks that we had monitoring the air and surface situation and monitoring the activities across the units that were not within the zone of responsibility of the VPS and not engaged in combat operations, most of the time we had to deal with a whole number of other tasks that we had to focus on gradually. We were receiving units that were being relocated from Croatia, units, manpower, military equipment and weapons, families, and their belongings. That was the main task, the principal task, and there was another task that we had to deal with. In some way, the operational centre became also an information centre, due to the fact that many soldiers were still in the barracks in Croatia, and we were receiving hundreds of calls on a daily basis from their mothers asking to be told about their sons, asking for information. This may seem as a trivial task, but for me it was a very important task, and I attached a lot of importance to this. I was nearly able to track down every single soldier, and I was nearly able to establish communication with each and every one of them via telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me about this relocation of the unit, of the military naval district, from Croatian territory. Was that an ongoing task throughout this period of time?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Yes, it was an ongoing task. And we were coordinators, this entire team that was appointed through the commander's order. We were coordinators, and we monitored the ships that carried out this transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were there any problems with the accommodation of the personnel involved, equipment, the families of these officers?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: There were major problems involved. It was chaos all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me: What was your personal feeling with regard to this entire situation in 1991, when all of this was taking place?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: For me, personally, it was a very difficult situation. I, as a human being, was, as our people say, between a rock and a hard place. On the one hand, I had the military oath that I made, and my wish to carry out my duties as an officer, according to the constitution. On the other hand, my own kin lived in Macedonia, and they were beseeching me to come back home. They were complaining. But my friends are mostly Croats, because my wife is originally Croatian. And they were telling me that I should leave the army altogether and that they would find me a job on a commercial ship. So that was what the situation was, and it was really hard for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the operations centre of the VPS in Kumbor, was there a logbook?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: There was an operations logbook, and there was this working map, so everything was entered into the logbook and into the working map, all the activities we had and unit movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me: What entries were made in the operations logbook at the peacetime command post in Kumbor?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: All the activities that took place on that day, all the orders that we would receive, then protests. That's it, for the most part. Everything that happened and everything that was important, we registered there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know whether there was a war logbook at the operations centre of the 9th VPS in Kupari?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: It was identical as it was where we were. This is in accordance with the rules and regulations that this kind of logbook and work map are kept in both places, that is to say, the logbook and the work map.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me: Do you know which operations officers worked at the forward command post Kupari of the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: I don't know. Well, it was warship Captain Kozaric; then Zarkovic, also warship captain; then Drljan, frigate captain; Dzelebdjic. I think he was a corvette captain. I can't remember exactly the rank he held then. And there were some officers who came from Belgrade too, but I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me: Did you ever work at the operations centre at the forward command post in Kupari?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Yes. From 1992 I went there, so I don't know whether it was February or some other month, but that's when I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please: Are you aware of any activities of the 9th Military Naval Sector on the date of the 6th of December, 1991? Around Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: I am aware of that. I don't know whether it was 9.00 or 10.00. It was in the morning, at any rate. We know that there was some activity going on there and that our forces had sustained losses, considerable losses. That's what we heard then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 6th of December, 1991, were you on duty at the operations centre in Kumbor?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Yes, I was present there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 6th of December, 1991, in Kumbor, did you have any contacts with the Dubrovnik side in relation to that situation?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, at one point in time I heard part of a conversation that Minister Rudolf had, I don't know with whom exactly, I just heard this one fragment, when he was complaining to someone in panic, or he was lodging or protest or something, concerning the forces that were on Srdj, that they saw a flag with a five-pointed star and then there were guns aimed at them. He said, and he said, "I personally see the guns aiming at us here and the population is in panic." That's what he said. And I think that there was some fire and that there were some casualties among them. That's what I heard. And I remember that fragment. It remained imprinted in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you remember perhaps the time period during the course of that day when you heard parts of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Well, as I said, 9.00, 10.00, up to 12.00. I cannot say exactly. But it was within that period, up to midday, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On that day, were there any other calls that were received at the operations centre in Kumbor that had to do with the situation in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Yes. There was a call that surprised me greatly, and perplexed me. Kadijevic called, General Kadijevic, and asked to speak to Admiral Jokic. I found him. I can't remember exactly. But at any rate, I found him, through the forward command post, and I put Kadijevic through. At that moment, I heard part of their conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it was that you heard?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: I can quote it. Perhaps it's the meaning that I can convey, the meaning will be conveyed completely, perhaps not the exact words. Kadijevic asked Jokic -- well, now I don't know on what terms they were. He said: "What are you doing down there?" Either in the singular or in the plural. "What are you doing down there? Do you know what you promised me when you asked to be sent down there?" As far as I can remember, Jokic said, in a rather confused manner, that he was just carrying out a tactical movement of units in order to correct the tactical deployment of the 9th VPS. That's what it was, along those lines. And then Kadijevic answered. He said: "We are making every effort here to topple Tudjman, and you are carrying out some kind of minor tactical movements." That is the conversation I heard, sort of. It's not a direct quotation, but this is definitely the meaning involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you hear this yourself?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Yes, I heard this myself. I held the receiver. I listened to the conversation. I heard that part of the conversation. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Do you remember in which period of time this conversation took place on the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Also in the morning, sometime before midday. Now was it at 10.00 or 11.00 or after that. But it was certainly before midday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know where your commander, Admiral Jokic, was on that day, the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: I know that all the time he was out there in Kupari or in Cavtat. After that, I know that he was supposed to go to Belgrade, and that day, sometime in the afternoon - I don't know exactly at what time - he took a helicopter from Cilipi to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Do you remember whether anyone from the 2nd Operational Group called the operations centre in Kumbor on that day?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no. No. Although sometimes I would go out for a few minutes or so, because at that time, on that day, what was characteristic for me was - and I remember this well - many families were coming and asking about their belongings. Because on the previous day, a ship had sunk on the previous day, and I know that some of the women were fainting, because they had all their belongings on those ships, including their cars and everything else. So then they would call me to the main gate so that I could explain to these people what had happened to the ship and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: The operations centre of the 9th Military Naval Sector in Kumbor, did it have any contacts during that period of time with the command of the Military Naval District?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: You mean that day? What day?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During that period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Yes, frequent ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for not switching the microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But what I asked you was about this period from October to December 1991, whether there were any contacts between the operations centre of the 9th VPS in Kumbor and the command of the military naval district.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Yes. They did have contacts, communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What was the relationship between, in the military sense, of course, in naval terms, the relationship between the 9th VPS and the military naval district?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That is not a matter to which this witness necessarily can testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you hear me?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We were the subordinate command to them. We were subordinate to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know any other subordinate command to the command of the military naval district?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Apart from the command of the 9th Military Naval Sector, did the military naval district have any other commands subordinated to it?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: It had the fleet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did it have anything else, any other commands?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: I don't think so, not during that period of time. Us and the fleet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were there any other military naval sectors within the military naval district?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Yes. There was the 8th, and Pula up there, the Pula one. That might have still been there, but it had already been abandoned, so I didn't count it as being under the command of the VP District. So those two military naval sectors weren't ours any more, in actual fact, didn't belong to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell us please: During that period of time - and I'm talking about October to December 1991 - did you receive any orders from the command of the military naval district at all?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: You mean by December, until December. Well, I think that we did receive something, an order about the relocation of units, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you have regular communication, daily communication with the command of the military naval district?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Well, practically every day, practically daily. And a helicopter would fly to Vis frequently. I think that's where the command was, on the island of Vis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And where was the command place of the military naval district otherwise?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Usually in Split, but in this case it was moved to the island of Vis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And with respect to the execution of orders, did you send out regular information to your superior command of the 9th Military Naval District -- I apologise. I meant the military naval district. Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Well, it was the forward command post, and we were just there in transit. We didn't deal with matters of this kind. The main command was at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, give us the location more precisely, where was that, the location of the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: The forward command post was in Kupari.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like the witness to be shown Exhibit D96, please. Mr. Handzijev, would you take a look at the document, please. Can you see it, what it's about, what kind of document it is? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: It's the war diary of the operations centre of the 9th VPS at the IKM, or forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would you take a look at page 66 now, please, the upper right-hand corner. You will find the number of the pages of the handwritten page. Have you found that page?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Take a look on the left -- at the left column and you will see the times, and this particular time I'm interested in is 1940 hours, that entry.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It is a message from the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik to the command of the VPS of Boka, asking them to confirm safe passage of the ship Argos II for the talks the next day that were scheduled to take place at 1000 hours in Cavtat and Crisis Staff's signature.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Yes, and that's normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And look at the entry for 1942 hours, that is to say, two minutes later. The command of the Military Naval Sector of Boka sending a message to the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik. We permit and guarantee the safe passage of the ship Argos II on the 6th of December, 1991, on the route between Dubrovnik harbour and Cavtat harbour and Dubrovnik harbour from 0900 hours until the ships arrived to the Dubrovnik harbour. The command of the 9th VPS. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And now take a look at the far right column, where it says "remarks." And here, under remarks, in the right-hand column, it says: "Convey to frigate captain Handzijev." Do you remember, although a lot of time has gone by since then, whether you ever received this message?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV
utterances.text: Well, they are standard types of messages. I can't say that I actually remember this particular one specifically, but yes, I do remember, generally speaking, what was going on, and this is standard practice. We might have had hundreds of messages like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. But what I'm interested in is this: When you look at the contents of this message at 1942 hours, as it is from the Military Naval Sector of Boka, the message sent to the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff, and that it was sent from the forward command post in Kupari, was it handed over to you, or rather, the operations centre in Kumbor, for you to send on further?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... could not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my question -- well, I understood him to say that he didn't remember this specific message, but this is a matter of the technique of sending out messages of this kind, the way in which this was done, the procedure. And I just asked him how it was handed further on, further down the line or up the line. If he's able to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I think he has said that he has no memory of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I'll move on. I don't know whether it's time for us to adjourn and end the proceedings for today. But at any rate, I'll complete shortly after we begin tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now, to resume tomorrow at 9.00. I must ask you if you would return tomorrow morning. We will be commencing again at 9.00 in the morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 9th day of July, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
